description: Linux Security Summit North America 2025 talks from Linux Security Summit North America 2025.

talks.title: Kernel Hardening: Ten Years Deep
talks.teaser: Reviews ten years of Linux kernel hardening, from bug-class elimination to compiler and allocator defenses against heap exploitation.
talks.summary:
The talk reviews ten years of the Linux kernel self-protection project, announced in 2015 to remove whole bug classes instead of patching flaws one at a time. The speaker presents lifetime analysis showing that kernel bugs often survived about five years before being fixed, and that the average lifetime of recently fixed flaws has started to fall. Lifetime statistics were drawn from Ubuntu's CVE tracker, and the speaker avoided mapping data across the February 2024 switch to kernel CNA assignments. Buffer overflows and integer overflows show declining counts, while use-after-free has become the main focus of attackers.

Most use-after-free exploitation relies on type confusion in the slab allocator, where objects of different sizes share size buckets. The talk traces defenses such as cgroup-separated accounting, randomized caches, and separate user-space buckets, then cross-cache attacks that return freed pages to the page allocator. Per-type virtual address regions and hardware memory tagging were described as partial answers, each with performance or coverage trade-offs.

Compiler work addresses the remaining gaps: zero-initialized stack variables, counted_by annotations that let bounds checks use runtime lengths, and a no-wrap attribute for unsigned arithmetic. Overflow checks were said to cost little at runtime, though code size grows. The takeaway is to push memory safety into the toolchain, coordinate language extensions across compilers, and write new code in Rust where possible.

talks.title: SeaBee: Defense for the Defense
talks.teaser: Explains how an open-source eBPF LSM framework isolates privileged security tools from tampering by other privileged processes.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by describing how eBPF and the eBPF LSM let verified programs hook kernel security decisions to enforce custom access controls at runtime. It argues that this model breaks down for privileged actors: anyone with eBPF capabilities can unload LSM programs or rewrite shared maps, so one tool’s policy cannot reliably confine other privileged loaders.

The core project, CB, is framed as a user-space daemon plus eBPF LSM programs that scope policies to loader binaries and their descendants, label objects with integer boundaries, and enforce map, program, filesystem, and process protections through specific LSM hooks. Administrators and tool owners interact through a CLI that submits signed policies over a Unix socket, tying each policy to cryptographic keys so only the original signer can update or remove it.

The talk closes by contrasting BPF token delegation with post-creation object isolation, noting out-of-scope threats like kernel compromise, and outlining limits such as missing BPF helpers for map security fields and verifier quirks. Practitioners gain a concrete open-source pattern for hardening eBPF-based security stacks on Linux without rebuilding distribution-wide SELinux policies.

talks.title: The State and Direction of LSM Stacking - Casey Schaufler, The Smack Project
talks.teaser: Survey of Linux kernel work to stack multiple security modules, from data blobs through audit, mount, and networking edges.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits a long-standing goal: running more than one major Linux security module at once instead of treating modules such as SELinux, App Armor, and Smack as mutually exclusive. Built-in modules execute in a fixed order, exclusive modules conflict on shared interfaces, and much of the stack still assumes a single “major” LSM—constraints that block practical cases like Android containers on Ubuntu that want both SELinux and App Armor policies active.

Progress centers on infrastructure cleanup rather than ad hoc patches. Security blobs are centralized so multiple modules can attach data to creds, inodes, and similar structures. LSM properties and LSM contexts replace brittle SEC ID assumptions and disambiguate textual contexts when two modules contribute labels. Auxiliary audit subject and object records avoid cramming multiple contexts into one field, with special handling when BPF LSM hooks are inactive until programs load. Mount option handling is being extended so unrecognized options can be claimed by another module, with dynamic blob allocation. Networking remains harder: secmark, NetLabel, CIPSO/CALIPSO, and getsockopt still effectively reserve one tag or mark for the first module in order, with proc-based UI clashes partly addressed via dedicated syscalls and per-LSM proc subtrees.

Shipping status includes merged or in-review work on properties, contexts, auxiliary audit records, and mount options, while NetLabel multi-tag and some context paths remain future work. Practitioners should expect ordering dependencies for audit rules, secmarks, and NetLabel until user space and tools catch up, especially for distributions and container stacks that must surface every module’s label in familiar utilities.

talks.title: Binding TDISP & Platform Attestation Reports for Confidential VMs
talks.teaser: Proposes binding TDISP device attestation evidence to platform attestation so verifiers can trust confidential VM devices.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short primer on confidential computing, which protects data in use inside hardware-backed trusted execution environments. It explains how TDISP lets a confidential VM attest a device and add it to its trusted computing base, so devices such as smart NICs can work on private memory directly instead of through encrypted bounce buffers. That removes the extra CPU work and cost of bounce buffers, though GPUs and crypto accelerators have been harder to support without it.

The speaker then sets platform attestation, a chain of trust from the CPU root of trust through firmware and the VM to the guest OS, against TDISP device attestation. The gap is that a remote verifier cannot tell whether device evidence came from the same CVM as the platform evidence, so an attacker could replay evidence from another VM and obtain secrets meant for a device-equipped one. The proposal extends a new virtual TPM NV index, which behaves like a PCR, with a digest of each device's evidence, records each extend in an event log, and signs the index with the vTPM attestation key already in the platform report. Defining the index in the platform hierarchy enables the delete-protection attribute so guests cannot redefine it.

The talk closes with open questions. Keeping a history of every device evaluated, including rejected ones, may bloat attestation requests and may need a configurable reset policy. It is also unclear where the event log and extend permissions should live, and whether only kernel drivers or applications too should be able to access them.

talks.title: SELinux All the Way Down: Namespaces for SELinux
talks.teaser: Explains kernel work that gives each container its own SELinux policy and enforcing mode, still confined by the host.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a proposed design for SELinux namespaces, which would let a container run its own SELinux policy instead of inheriting the single system-wide policy of its host. Today a container usually sees SELinux as disabled, and the host treats every process in it as one label, so fine-grained labeling inside containers is not possible and developers must test with full virtual machines. The goal is to run stock distribution containers, and eventually Android, with enforcing policy while preventing escape to the host.

Each namespace gets its own policy, access vector cache, enforcing mode and SELinux filesystem instance, and it stays confined by every ancestor up to the host's initial namespace. Permission checks walk up that chain, and per-namespace process labels are tracked through credentials, with global SIDs replacing per-policy identifiers. Namespace count and nesting depth are limited and can only be set from the initial namespace, and unsharing is requested through a SELinux filesystem node. The speaker demonstrated a systemd-nspawn proof of concept that booted an enforcing Fedora container, and reported that the kernel test suite passed in a child namespace apart from some labeled networking tests, with benchmarks showing no significant overhead.

Before upstreaming, two items remain: finalizing the unshare interface so user space does not break later, and minimizing overhead in the default case. Other gaps include per-namespace mount options, label mapping, network and audit namespacing, and untested Android, Ubuntu and Debian containers. Tested cases so far covered Fedora and Rocky containers on Fedora and Ubuntu hosts, so this is early-stage kernel work for practitioners to watch.

talks.title: Handling New Syscalls in Seccomp Filters
talks.teaser: Tom Hromatka analyzes Handling New Syscalls in Seccomp Filters.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, libseccomp maintainer Tom Hromatka (joined by co-maintainer Paul Moore) presents a proposed patch set designed to handle newly introduced Linux system calls in seccomp filters. When kernel updates introduce unfamiliar syscalls, static allow lists or deny lists can lead to unexpected security holes or broken applications. The proposed feature introduces kernel version awareness into libseccomp, allowing developers to define a target maximum kernel version and specify dedicated actions for any syscall introduced after that version.

### Key Topics
- **Allow Lists vs. Deny Lists**: Seccomp filters typically use either deny lists (blocking specific calls and allowing the rest, common in containers like Docker) or allow lists (blocking by default). With deny lists, kernel updates may unintentionally permit brand-new, potentially vulnerable syscalls; with allow lists, new syscalls needed by updated libraries (such as glibc) are blocked, causing container and application failures.
- **Upgrade Hesitancy**: Administrators and container operators frequently delay kernel and user-space updates out of fear that new syscall additions will break production workloads.
- **Proposed Filter Attributes**: The patch set introduces two new opt-in libseccomp filter attribute enumerations. These enable users to define the maximum kernel version their filter was validated against (with logic going back as far as Linux 3.0) and choose an explicit fallback action (such as returning `ENOSYS`) for any syscall introduced in subsequent kernel releases.
- **Filter Size and Generation Challenges**: Because Linux syscall numbers have historically not been assigned strictly sequentially across architectures and distributions often backport calls irregularly, libseccomp currently generates checks on a per-syscall basis rather than simple numeric ranges, impacting the resulting classic BPF filter size.

### Technical Details
- **BPF Generation & Data Structures**: libseccomp maintains a two-dimensional in-memory table mapping architectures, syscalls, and the Linux kernel version in which each syscall was introduced. When compiling into classic BPF (or pseudo filter code / PFC for human inspection), it evaluates whether a syscall matches explicitly handled rules, falls back to default actions for known calls, or triggers the new-syscall action for calls newer than the configured kernel version.
- **Sequential vs. Enumerated Matching**: While tools like runc have implemented range checks assuming syscall numbers greater than a certain threshold are new, libseccomp takes a cautious approach by enumerating syscalls individually to account for irregular numbering across 20+ architectures. To mitigate performance overhead from hundreds of instructions, libseccomp employs optimizations such as binary search trees.
- **Action Choices**: Returning `ENOSYS` is recommended for unsupported new syscalls, as user-space runtimes and libraries often cleanly fall back to older syscall interfaces (e.g., falling back to earlier `openat` variants). However, some enterprise environments have hard requirements such as killing the process immediately.

### Takeaways
- The proposed kernel-version-aware handling is an entirely opt-in mechanism configured via libseccomp filter attributes.
- Setting the default action for unknown/new syscalls to `ENOSYS` solves compatibility issues for the majority of users, though documentation and education remain crucial.
- Maintainers are gathering community feedback on the API design, table accuracy, and potential hybrid approaches (such as combining strict per-syscall lookups with range checks) before merging.

talks.title: Layered Attestation of a Cross-Domain System
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Layered Attestation of a Cross-Domain System - Perry Alexander, University of Kansas.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Perry Alexander from the University of Kansas presents work developed alongside students, MITRE collaborators (Josh Guttman, Paul Rowe), and NSA colleagues (Jim Carter, Steve Smalley, Daniel DeGraaf) on building an end-to-end, layered semantic remote attestation architecture. The goal of the project was to construct a functioning system spanning from hardware boot through runtime measurement and empirical testing. To validate their approach, the team targeted a realistic, third-party cross-domain email cleansing pipeline written in OCaml, designing an attestation framework that binds boot-time guarantees directly to runtime evidence collection.

### Key Topics
- **Layered Architecture & Roots of Trust:** Grounded in principles outlined by Coker et al., the system builds upward from a hardware root of trust (TPM 2.0 and EFI firmware) through an operating system layer (Linux, SELinux, IMA), up to a Measurement and Attestation (M&A) subsystem, and ultimately the target application.
- **Attestation Manager & Copeland Language:** Attestation workflows are specified using the Copeland attestation protocol language and executed by a formally verified attestation manager within the Maestro framework.
- **The Attestation Manager Signing Key:** A foundational mechanism linking boot state to runtime attestation by sealing an attestation manager signing key to specific TPM Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs).
- **Design for Attestation:** Structuring target software components (such as rewrite and filter stages) to start, process, and terminate rather than running persistent daemon processes, significantly simplifying runtime state appraisal by shifting the verification burden to configuration files and static binaries.
- **Empirical Attack Testing & Analysis:** Using MITRE's Chase tool to enumerate protocol attack paths and validate detection capabilities against configuration and binary tampering.

### Technical Details
- **Boot Chain and PCR Measurements:** EFI firmware initializes measurement into PCR 4 (bootloader), while the bootloader measures initramfs into PCR 9 and the command line into PCR 8. Inside initramfs, a specialized script hashes the IMA policy and SELinux policy into PCR 11. PCR 10 is populated by IMA but excluded from sealing due to unpredictable runtime variation.
- **Key Protection and Sealing:** The attestation manager signing key blob resides in user space, protected by SELinux and IMA. The key is sealed to PCRs 4, 8, 9, and 11 in the TPM 2.0. The TPM unseals and loads the key only if the bootloader, initramfs, command line, and security policies match expected values. Consequently, any signature produced with this key cryptographically proves that the attestation manager ran on a correctly booted system.
- **Measurement Pipeline:** The runtime protocol invokes Attestation Service Providers (ASPs) strictly ordered via Copeland sequential semantics: first verifying kernel/SELinux integrity with Invariant Corporation's LKIM (Linux Kernel Integrity Measurement) tool, appraising running SELinux policy, hashing configuration files, and finally hashing statically linked application binaries before signing the evidence bundle. ASPs are constrained to read-only operations and verified via IMA.

### Takeaways & Future Directions
- **Formal Verification Benefits:** Formally verifying the compact attestation manager proved far more tractable than verifying complex target applications, ensuring that Copeland protocols execute with strict fidelity.
- **Bridging Boot and Runtime:** Binding user-space signing capabilities directly to TPM-sealed PCR states provides a robust bridge from boot-time measurements to runtime attestation bundles.
- **Open Challenges:** Significant engineering challenges remain in provisioning and distributing known-good reference hashes across heterogeneous hardware, managing updates/live patching without breaking PCR states, conducting runtime memory introspection for dynamic processes, and scaling layered attestation across broader enterprise environments.
